newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean strike call draws limited response.
newsitem.headline: South Korean strike call draws limited response.

text.p: South Korean workers responded half-heartedly on Wednesday to a strike call by an outlawed union group following President Kim Young-sam's stunning retreat over a controversial labour law.

The Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which said it was disappointed by Kim's decision to send the legislation back to parliament for debate, insisted the government scrap the law before it takes affect on March 1 and come up with a new bill.

The ruling New Korea party rammed the law through parliament during a dawn session on December 26 while opposition deputies slept, sparking more than three weeks of wildcat strikes that hit key sectors of the export-led economy.

Police picked up a leader from the confederation but later released him in line with Kim's new spirit of compromise over the law, which lets companies sack employees, replace strikers and introduce flexible work hours.
Dan Byong-ho was one of seven confederation leaders holed up at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral. He was detained for two hours of questioning near the capital, a state prosecutor said.
Police have withdrawn a security cordon from the church following Kim's order to suspend arrest warrants served on confederation leaders directing strikes from a ramshackle tent.
A confederation leader declined to say how long the unionists would stay on the cathedral grounds.
President Kim's dramatic climbdown on Tuesday followed a decision by the confederation to call off indefinite stoppages and limit industrial action to one day each week.
The Labour Ministry said 68,500 workers from the country's 12-million strong workforce observed the strike call. It said this was mainly confined to the automobile industry.
The confederation said about 140,000 workers downed tools.
In a statement, it also repeated the union's threat to call out all its 500,000 members for an indefinite strike from February 18 if the law was not repealed.

In a major concession to the opposition during a meeting of the heads of the three main political parties on Tuesday, Kim conceded the law had caused public anxiety and had damaged the economy. He agreed to send it back to parliament.
Analysts have said Kim was also bowing to public criticism over the forced passage of the law, with many commentators comparing his tactics to those of previous military rulers.
But Kim, who argues the law would free up the labour market and trim company costs as well as boost competitiveness, said dumping the legislation would go against the constitution.
Up until his stunning about-face, he had refused to even meet opposition leaders to discuss the law.
Bill Jordan, head of the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, told a news conference at the cathedral that Kim's move was a step in the right direction.

"We were very encouraged by that development, but we do believe the crisis was precipitated by the introduction of the law on December 26 and that the air of crisis affecting Korea could be removed by its nullification," he said.
Jordan is leading a 10-member delegation of world labour leaders in a show of solidarity for the unionists.
Stocks slid on fears the reversal would delay restructuring of the economy, brokers said. The main index fell a provisional 11.60 points, or 1.68 percent, to close the day at 678.94.
A Hyundai Motor Co Ltd union official in the southeastern city of Ulsan said 29,000 confederation members had joined the strike and that production would be halted for one day.
But Lee Chung-tak, a company public relations officer, said although production was slow, the factory was still running.
A union official from Ulsan-based Hyundai Heavy Industries, the nation's largest shipyard, said only 210 workers had joined the stoppages. Production would not be affected, he said.
Union members at automaker Kia Motors, located just outside Seoul, held partial strikes in the afternoon.
During the meeting on Tuesday, Kim expressed sorrow for the loss of billions of dollars in output through the strikes.
He also agreed to reopen debate on another controversial law reviving a once-notorious domestic spy agency.
According to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung of the National Congress for New Politics, the president also indicated that the confederation should be recognised.
